The problem

Removing access is easy to describe as a permissions change. The harder question is what the organization can no longer do afterward. A role might be the only thing keeping a time-sensitive business workflow covered.

RoleImpact explores that gap by linking employees, roles, permissions, capabilities, and workflow requirements in a single model.

My contribution

I built the React and TypeScript interface, Spring Boot API, object-oriented Java impact-analysis logic, and PostgreSQL persistence for this portfolio project. The work connects an interactive simulation workflow to explainable backend results.

From change to consequence

A reviewer opens an example organization, removes a role, and follows the relationship paths to affected workflows. They can then test a proposed replacement and compare the original impact with the mitigated result.

The analysis is deterministic. Recommendations come from explicit eligibility and workflow rules, rather than an opaque model score.

Architecture

  • React + TypeScript: organization exploration, impact maps, and before-and-after comparisons.
  • Java 21 & Spring Boot: microservices for simulations, draft previews, and organization data.
  • Apache Kafka: asynchronous event-driven messaging to decouple simulation processing and support scalable backend execution.
  • Deterministic Java impact engine: evaluates changes against versioned snapshots, stable result hashing, and ranks eligible mitigation options.
  • PostgreSQL + JPA + Flyway: persistent catalog data, saved simulation relationships, and versioned schema migrations.
  • JUnit + Testcontainers: integration testing against real PostgreSQL container instances to verify persistence and REST API behaviour.

Engineering challenges

A replacement recommendation must do more than match a role name. It must respect the workflow constraints and actually restore coverage. Keeping simulation inputs immutable makes original and alternative scenarios comparable.

The interface also needs to explain a relationship-rich result without making the graph the only way to understand it. The project includes textual relationship paths alongside the visual map.

Result and scope

The application demonstrates an end-to-end path from an access change to an impact explanation and a tested mitigation, with persistent organization data and draft previews.

This is a portfolio simulator using synthetic examples. It does not connect to identity providers or provision real permissions. Editable examples are not a place for confidential organizational data.

What the project taught me

The central design lesson is that explainability belongs in the data model and engine contracts. A useful result includes the relationship path and rule behind the outcome, so the interface can show why a workflow is affected.
